title: Quantitative Skills
text:
Welcome to the Quantitative Skills strand of GEOG0187 Foundations of Geography II. This term has three parts:

Spatial Data Collection. Before the field trip to Catalonia, you prepare to collect your own spatial data: the routes you walk and the sites you record.
Mapping. After the trip, you map your field data in ArcGIS Online, turn it into a story map, and learn to work with and evaluate secondary data.
Statistics. Finally, you use R to describe data, quantify uncertainty, and compare groups.




Moodle is the central point of contact for GEOG0187 and it is where all important information will be communicated, such as session dates, group allocations and assessment information. This workbook contains the material for the Quantitative Skills sessions.



Each session starts with a short introduction, after which you work through the material in this workbook at your own pace, with Affiliate Lecturers and Teaching Assistants on hand to help. Some sessions ask you to do a short task before you come to class: this is flagged at the top of the relevant chapter.



The topics are listed below. Chapters are released ahead of each session; check Moodle for the exact dates.

title: 1 Collecting Spatial Data
text:
On the field trip to Catalonia your group will collect its own spatial data: the route you walk, and the sites you record for your Urban Project. After the trip, in the Mapping sessions, you will put these data on a map, combine them with other data, and build a story map. Data you do not collect in Catalonia cannot be collected afterwards, so this week is about making sure everything works before you travel.






ImportantBefore the session: set up and test walk



Work through Before the session below. It takes about 20 minutes, most of it walking. There is nothing to hand in: just bring your phone, with your test walk saved in Strava, to the session.




Almost everything geographers study happens somewhere. Spatial data record not only what something is, but also where it is. A photo of a street vendor is data; the same photo together with the coordinates of where it was taken is spatial data, because it can be placed on a map and related to everything else around it: the route you walked, the neighbourhood it sits in, or census statistics for that area.
Most spatial data take one of three basic shapes:

Points: a single location, such as a site you record or a bus stop.
Lines: a sequence of locations, such as the route you walk.
Polygons: an area with a boundary, such as a neighbourhood or a census district.

Locations are stored as coordinates: latitude, the position north or south of the equator, and longitude, the position east or west of the meridian through Greenwich. Plaça de Catalunya in Barcelona, for instance, is at about 41.387° N, 2.170° E. Your phone works out its coordinates from satellite positioning (GPS). Outdoors this is typically accurate to within 5 to 10 metres, but it gets worse between tall buildings and indoors, which is worth keeping in mind when you record sites in narrow streets.
A geographic information system (GIS) is software for storing, combining, analysing and mapping spatial data. Because every record has a location, a GIS can overlay datasets that were collected separately, such as your sites, your route, a street map and census data, and help answer questions about where things happen and what is near what. In this module we use ArcGIS Online, a GIS that runs in your web browser.



Your group collects two datasets: your route as a line, and your sites as points. You collect each with a different tool:



What
Tool
How it works




Your route
Strava
A phone app that records your GPS track in the background, also without mobile data. You export it afterwards as a .gpx file.


Your sites
UCL Geography Field Survey
A web form that opens in your phone’s browser. Each entry records your location, a photo and a short note, and goes straight into ArcGIS Online, so there is no copying of coordinates by hand.



Everyone records the route on their own phone, so you each end up with your own copy and nothing is lost if one phone runs out of battery. Sites only need to be submitted once per working group, so you will agree who does that.






NoteIf your screen looks different



Apps and websites change their layout regularly. This chapter therefore describes what to tap by its label (e.g. Record) rather than showing screenshots. If a label has moved or been renamed, look for the closest equivalent, and ask in class if you cannot find it.





Do this in the week before the session.



Install Strava from the App Store or Google Play and create a free account. You do not need a paid subscription. Remember your login details: you will need them on the Strava website later.
When asked, allow location access While Using the App.
Make your activities private: tap the You tab, then the settings cog (top right), and go to Privacy Controls → Activities → Only You. You can still export private activities.





Both Strava and your web browser (for the field survey) need access to your location. On an iPhone, both settings are under Settings → Apps:

Strava: Settings → Apps → Strava → Location. Select While Using the App and keep Precise Location switched on.

Safari: Settings → Apps → Safari, then scroll a long way down to Location. Select Allow or Ask, not Deny.


On Android, go to Settings → Apps → Strava → Permissions → Location, choose Allow only while using the app and switch on Use precise location. Do the same for Chrome.




Open the UCL Geography Field Survey on your phone. It opens in your browser; there is nothing to install.
Sign in with your UCL account. If you are asked for Your ArcGIS organization’s URL, type uclondon, tap Continue, then UCL SSO, and sign in as you would for Moodle. You do not need to fill in the survey yet.
Add it to your home screen so you can find it quickly in the field: in Safari use Share → Add to Home Screen; in Chrome use the ⋮ menu → Add to Home screen.





Somewhere outside, open Strava, tap Record, choose Walk as the activity type, and start. You can lock your phone; Strava keeps recording.
Walk for about 10 minutes.
Stop Strava (Stop → Finish), name the activity GEOG0187 test walk, and Save it.
Check that your route looks right on the map, and notice how much battery the walk used.





Your phone, charged, with the test walk saved in Strava.
Your Strava login details.
Anything that did not work, or that you were unsure about.





We start with a live demonstration: your Affiliate Lecturer has done the same test walk with the same instructions, and will show how to get the route out of Strava, how to fill in the field survey, and what the data look like in ArcGIS Online. You then do the same:

Export your test walk. The .gpx file can only be downloaded from the Strava website, not from the app, so use a laptop or computer. Log in at strava.com, open your test walk, open the ⋯ (more actions) menu next to the activity and choose Export GPX. Check that a .gpx file has been downloaded. 
Try the field survey. Open the survey from your home screen and submit one test entry from the room:

Data collection: select Fieldwork - Test.
Group number: 0.
Site ID: S00.
Location: tap Allow when asked, and check the dot on the map is roughly where you are. If it is off, wait a few seconds or drag it to the right spot.
Photo and a short note: anything will do.
Tap Submit and check that you see a confirmation. 

Fix problems. Work through anything that did not work with the people around you and with staff. The troubleshooting table covers the most common issues.
Plan as a working group. Agree who submits the sites (one or two people, so that each site is entered only once) and who takes over if their phone runs out of battery. Agree how your sites relate to your Urban Project theme.
Agree on site IDs. Number your sites S01, S02, S03, and so on, per group, and use the same ID everywhere: in the survey, in your field notebook, and in the names or captions of any extra photos, videos or audio. This is what lets you match your notes to your points later.

By the end of the session everyone should have exported a .gpx file and submitted one test entry from their own phone.




Everyone starts Strava when your group starts walking, and stops it when you finish. One recording per outing is fine; you can have several.
Submit one survey entry per site, while you are standing at the site, with Data collection set to your fieldwork group (not Fieldwork - Test) and your own working group number.
Charge your phone every night and bring a power bank if you have one. GPS and the camera use a lot of battery.
No signal or no mobile data? Strava keeps recording without data and uploads when you are back online. The survey needs a connection to submit: if you have none, take a photo with your camera, note the site ID and time in your notebook, and submit the entry later, placing the point by dragging the dot to the right location on the map. Check your phone contract for roaming charges before you go.
Be considerate. Avoid photos in which people can be identified, and follow the ethics guidance in your Urban Project worksheet. Do not record your accommodation as a site.




Your sites are already in ArcGIS Online. Before the next session:

Export your own route. Download the .gpx file(s) of your recordings from the Strava website, as in the session. If your recording failed, ask someone in your working group for a copy of theirs.
Share everything else. Put extra photos, videos and notes in a shared OneDrive or Google Drive folder for your working group. Avoid WhatsApp for photos: it compresses them and removes their location information.











Problem
What to try




Strava does not record, or the route is a straight line
Check location access is set to While Using the App with Precise Location on. Do not force-close the app while recording. Turn off Low Power Mode if the route has gaps.


No Export GPX option
Use the Strava website on a laptop, not the app or a phone browser. You can only export your own activities.


The survey asks me to sign in again
Sign in as in the setup: organisation URL uclondon, then UCL SSO. You may need to do this again after a while, also in Catalonia.


The survey cannot find my location
Allow location for your browser (see above), then reload the form. Indoors or between tall buildings it can take a little while; step into the open.


The point is in the wrong place
Drag the dot on the map to the correct location before submitting.


No confirmation after Submit
Check you have a connection, then tap Submit again. Required fields that are missing are highlighted in the form.


Photo will not upload
Try again on wifi, or submit without the photo and note the site ID on the photo instead.
